summary: For ages 10-11: build the argument that most of a plant's growing mass comes from air (carbon dioxide) and water, not from the soil it grows in. The whole topic is an argument-from-evidence against the durable 'plants eat soil' intuition, anchored on the classic mass-balance (van Helmont) evidence: a plant gains kilograms while its soil loses only grams. Keep the mechanism light at this level (materials come from air and water); the CO2 to glucose chemistry belongs to a later stage.
misconceptions: 'Plants get their food/mass from the soil' — the dominant, tenacious misconception this topic exists to demolish.
Believing a plant's wood/mass comes mostly from water alone, omitting the air (CO2) contribution.
Thinking air can't be 'material' because it's invisible and weightless (so it couldn't build a tree).
Assuming soil minerals are the plant's food rather than small quantities for health.
Confusing where WATER comes from (soil) with where the bulk MATERIAL comes from (air + water) — conceding water-from-soil then wrongly extending to all mass.
Treating the claim as something to memorise rather than something the mass-balance evidence proves.

activities.title: Where does a tree come from? A mass-balance investigation
steps: First, before any data, answer aloud or in writing: 'A tiny sapling grows into a huge tree weighing tens of kilograms. Where did all that extra wood and leaf material come from?' Record your honest prediction (most learners say 'from the soil').
Record starting masses: a pot of dried soil (e.g. 90.000 kg) and a tiny sapling (e.g. 2 kg).

Over the growing period, add nothing to the pot but water, and cover the soil so dust or fallen leaves can't change its mass. Then re-weigh both the grown plant and the soil, drying the soil again first so that differences in how wet it is don't hide the result (e.g. tree now 77 kg; soil now 89.943 kg).
Compute and compare the two changes side by side: plant gained about +75 kg; soil lost only about 57 g (-0.057 kg).
Try to answer 'where did the ~75 kg come from?' by proposing soil as the source, then test that idea against the numbers: the soil barely changed, so it cannot account for ~75 kg.

Reveal and state the source: invisible carbon dioxide taken from the air, plus water. Note that the weighing rules out soil but cannot by itself tell air from water (van Helmont himself concluded the mass came from water). The extra clue is that much of a plant's dry material is carbon, which carbon dioxide contains and water does not. Write a claim-evidence-reasoning statement: CLAIM (mass comes chiefly from air and water); EVIDENCE (plant +75 kg while soil only -57 g; plant material contains carbon, and carbon dioxide in the air is the carbon source); REASONING (if the soil had supplied the mass it would have lost kilograms, so the mass came from elsewhere; the other inputs were water and air, and the carbon must have come from the air).
activities.insight: A growing plant gains far more mass than the soil loses, so the soil cannot be the source of that mass. The weighing alone doesn't separate air from water, but the carbon in plant material shows that carbon dioxide from the air contributes along with water. This is an argument from evidence, not a fact to memorise.

activities.title: Simulated mass-balance with live readouts (optional interactive version)
steps: On a digital scale, weigh the soil and sapling to set starting values.
Drag a time slider across several years while adding only water; watch the sapling grow into a substantial tree.
Re-weigh everything; two readouts animate side by side - e.g. TREE +75 kg vs SOIL -57 g.
Respond to the prompt 'where did the mass come from?' by dragging a candidate source (soil / air / water) into the balance; a 'soil' choice is refuted because the soil readout barely moved.
Toggle to reveal carbon dioxide (from air) + water as the material, then assemble the claim-evidence-reasoning panel.
activities.insight: Compressing a years-long experiment into seconds is intended to let the learner personally generate and confront the kilograms-gained-versus-grams-lost gap, so the air+water conclusion can land as a genuine surprise.

activities.title: Defend the claim against a skeptic
steps: Face a skeptical partner (or role-play one) who insists 'the tree's wood obviously came from the soil it grew in - convince me otherwise.'
Marshal the mass-balance evidence out loud: state the figures (plant +kg, soil -grams) and reason that the soil could not be the source.
Respond to follow-up challenges: 'Carbon dioxide is a gas - how can a gas become solid wood?' and 'A gardener adds plant food to the pot - isn't that where the mass comes from?'
Keep arguing until the skeptic concedes only to sound reasoning.
activities.insight: Defending the claim aloud - not just recognising the right answer - rehearses the argue-from-evidence practice and can surface any residual 'soil' or 'water-only' thinking.

activities.title: Separate the minerals from the mass; bridge to photosynthesis
steps: Draw an arrow model: CO2 (from air) + water (from soil) -> plant material, with soil minerals shown as a thin side-arrow.
Explain in a sentence the different jobs: water comes from the soil (and is a source of material); air supplies carbon dioxide; soil minerals come in small amounts for health, not bulk.
State the forward link lightly: the invisible air gas plus water become the plant's food and structure (this is photosynthesis), without writing any chemical equation.
activities.insight: Water coming from the soil does not mean all the mass comes from the soil; minerals are a tiny health contribution, and the bulk material is CO2 + water. This sets up photosynthesis without overreaching the mechanism.

checkQuestion: A tiny seedling is planted in a pot of soil and grows over years into a huge plant weighing many kilograms. If I weighed the soil at the start and again years later, the soil would have lost only a few grams. So where did all the plant's extra mass come from? Explain your reasoning.
checkAnswer: Most of the plant's mass comes from the AIR (carbon dioxide) and WATER, not from the soil. In photosynthesis the leaves use light to build food (and the plant's body) from CO₂ taken from the air and water — that's why a huge plant can grow while the soil barely changes. Full marks locate the mass in air+water and use the barely-changed soil as the evidence.
